name: Othello error
statement: Signs of stress in a truthful person under suspicion look like signs of stress in a liar, and an observer who reads them as guilt condemns the innocent.
meaning: The claim is about inference, not about behaviour. It has two links. The first is that an innocent person who knows she is being doubted has something to be afraid of, namely not being believed, and that fear produces the same display as the fear of being caught. The second is that a lie catcher who observes the display attributes it to the only cause he is entertaining. Paul Ekman's group puts the first link plainly: the fear of being disbelieved when innocent looks the same as the fear of being caught when guilty. It puts the second as the point that observing an emotion does not tell you what caused it. Shakespeare supplies the name. Othello read Desdemona's fear as the reaction of a woman caught in betrayal, and the reading was self-confirming because his own accusation produced the fear. Ekman's companion warning, the Brokaw hazard, concerns a different failure: taking a behaviour for a clue to deceit when it is a habit of the particular person. The Othello error is not the claim that nervousness never separates liars from truth tellers. It is the claim that a display of nervousness is consistent with two histories, and that suspicion itself supplies the innocent one.

origin.note: The book is a trade work of synthesis and reports no experiment on this point. Its text could not be read during this check, because the 1985 scan at the Internet Archive is lending-restricted and the HathiTrust copy is search-only behind a challenge page. The attribution of the phrase to the 1985 book is taken from Tummon, Allen and Bindemann, who cite it as Ekman 1985/2001. The definition quoted on this page is the wording published by the Paul Ekman Group.

evidence: Bond and Fahey put the prediction to an experiment two years after the book, without using its name. Their abstract states the hypothesis as truth tellers looking dishonest when suspected of lying. It reports that the experiment found evidence of this error in truth detection. It adds that the error reflects a seeming confirmation of false accusations rather than a perceptual distortion. The sender side of the chain is weak. DePaulo and colleagues pooled 1,338 estimates of 158 cues across 120 independent samples and found liars more nervous and tense overall than truth tellers by d = 0.27, 95% confidence interval 0.16 to 0.38, from 16 estimates and 571 participants. The median absolute effect across 88 cues was 0.10, and two reached 0.50. Their own reading of what this means for stress is direct. Nervousness discriminates in a murder trial only if liars feel more nervous than truth tellers there. It discriminates better than in traffic court only if that gap widens with the stakes. Raising the stakes did widen it for some cues, with overall tension at d = 0.35 under motivation against 0.15 without it, and pitch at 0.59 against -0.02. Hartwig and Bond synthesised 144 samples covering 9,380 senders and 26,866 messages. Their abstract reports that lies can be detected from constellations of cues with nearly 70% accuracy, and that this level is stable across settings. Vrij, Hartwig and Granhag read that stability as the Othello prediction holding at scale. They write that the same meta-analysis found no effect for strong emotion and none for motivation. The reason they give is that liars may show more nervous behaviour when the stakes are high but so may truth tellers, and they cite Bond and Fahey for it. The observer side has been measured too. Meissner and Kassin found that neither training nor investigative experience improved discrimination, and that both shifted response bias towards answering deceit rather than truth. The applied cost is set out in the National Research Council's polygraph review. It works through a hypothetical population of 10,000 examinees containing 10 spies, at an accuracy index of 0.90. A test set sensitively enough to detect about 80 percent or more of deceivers would fail about 1,606 employees or more. The review concludes that polygraph testing yields an unacceptable choice between too many loyal employees falsely judged deceptive and too many major security threats left undetected.

replication.headline: No study testing the Othello error under that name was found, and no repetition of Bond and Fahey's 1987 experiment was found either.
replication.detail: Searches described in limits returned no empirical paper that names the Othello error and tests it. The phrase returns four full-text hits in the Europe PMC corpus: a machine-learning review, a lie-transfer study, an essay on the evolution of deception and a virtual-reality passport study. All four use it to explain a result rather than to test a prediction. Bond and Fahey's experiment is the direct test located here, and nothing citing it as a replication target was found. What has been repeated is the surrounding measurement, and it cuts two ways. The senders' side is weaker than Ekman's account needs, with nervousness separating liars from truth tellers by about a quarter of a standard deviation. Vrij, Hartwig and Granhag conclude from the meta-analytic pattern that the emotional theory is not well supported, nervousness and tenseness being the only two cues weakly related to deception. The observers' side is not obviously the misattribution Ekman described. Hartwig and Bond correlated 66 behavioural cues across 153 samples with deception judgments. Judgments were strongly tied to impressions of incompetence, r = .59, and ambivalence, r = .49, and only weakly to eye contact, r = -.15. Comparing cues to perceived deception with cues to actual deception, they found the two sets covarying at r = .59 and r = .72. Their conclusion is that people rarely rely on the wrong cues, and that accuracy is limited by the weakness of the cues themselves. Luke and colleagues surveyed 50 active deception researchers against an 80% threshold for consensus. Only gaze aversion cleared it. Around 70% agreed that liars and truth tellers do not differ in nervous behaviour, which the authors flag as hard to square with the meta-analytic estimate, noting that no body of work has shown the effect to be near zero.

limits: The founding text was not read. Everything on this page about what Ekman wrote comes from the Paul Ekman Group's published wording and from a peer-reviewed paper citing the book, and neither states which pages carry the term. Bond and Fahey is quoted from the abstract deposited at Crossref; the article sits behind a paywall, so the sample size, the design and the size of the effect are all absent here. Two claims in the evidence section reach this page at one remove. The finding that Hartwig and Bond's 2014 meta-analysis showed no moderation by emotion or by motivation is quoted from Vrij, Hartwig and Granhag's description of it, not from the meta-analysis, whose text was not obtained. The same review reports an experiment by Vrij in 1995 in which nonverbal cues to deceit appeared in an information-gathering interview and not in an accusatory one, and that experiment was not retrieved. Hatz and Bourgeois's 'Anger as a cue to truthfulness' tests a related Ekman prediction about falsely accused truth tellers; it was located and not read, and nothing about its result is stated here. The search for a named test covered Crossref bibliographic queries, Europe PMC full-text search for the exact phrase, and general web search. Europe PMC indexes open-access and biomedical work, and most of the deception literature sits in psychology journals outside it, so a named test in a paywalled communication or law journal would not show up in any of the three. The polygraph figures are illustrative arithmetic from an assumed accuracy index rather than field measurements, and the report presents them as such.
misreadings: The commonest reading is that nervousness carries no information about deception. The pooled estimate is small and positive, d = 0.27 with a 95% interval from 0.16 to 0.38, and Luke and colleagues point out that no study has established the effect at zero. The second reading is that lie catchers are looking at the wrong things. Hartwig and Bond's lens-model analysis found that the cues observers use track the cues that actually differ, and located the failure in how faint those cues are rather than in observers' choice of them. Ekman's error can survive that finding, because a faint valid cue read confidently is exactly the mistake described, but the version of the error that blames untutored intuition does not survive it. A third reading turns the error into a general tendency to call people liars. Across the ordinary run of experiments the bias runs the other way, towards believing what is said, as the truth-default entry sets out. The deceit-side bias appears in trained investigators, where Meissner and Kassin found it with no matching gain in accuracy. A fourth reading takes Hartwig and Bond's nearly 70% as what human judges achieve. It is the accuracy of a statistical model fitted to constellations of behavioural cues, which is the ceiling those cues allow rather than the score people get.

sources.text: Ekman, P. (1985). Telling Lies: Clues to Deceit in the Marketplace, Politics, and Marriage. New York: W. W. Norton. The record for the 1985 printing; the scan is lending-restricted and the text was not read for this entry.
Paul Ekman Group. Errors in detecting lies: the Othello error and the Brokaw hazard. Source for the wording of both errors quoted on this page.

Tummon, H. M., Allen, J., & Bindemann, M. (2020). Body language influences on facial identification at passport control: an exploration in virtual reality. i-Perception, 11(5). Cited only for its attribution of the term to Ekman 1985/2001.

Bond, C. F., Jr., & Fahey, W. E. (1987). False suspicion and the misperception of deceit. British Journal of Social Psychology, 26(1), 41-46. Quoted from the abstract deposited at Crossref; the article was not retrieved.

DePaulo, B. M., Lindsay, J. J., Malone, B. E., Muhlenbruck, L., Charlton, K., & Cooper, H. (2003). Cues to deception. Psychological Bulletin, 129(1), 74-118. All figures here are read off the article text.
Hartwig, M., & Bond, C. F. (2011). Why do lie-catchers fail? A lens model meta-analysis of human lie judgments. Psychological Bulletin, 137(4), 643-659. Quoted from the abstract at PubMed.

Hartwig, M., & Bond, C. F. (2014). Lie detection from multiple cues: a meta-analysis. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 28(5), 661-676. Quoted from the abstract deposited at Crossref; its moderator results are quoted here from Vrij, Hartwig and Granhag (2019).

Vrij, A., Hartwig, M., & Granhag, P. A. (2019). Reading lies: nonverbal communication and deception. Annual Review of Psychology, 70(1), 295-317. Source for the moderator nulls and for the Vrij (1995) interview finding, both at one remove.

Luke, T. J., Mac Giolla, E., Memon, A., Landström, S., Granhag, P. A., & Kassin, S. M. (2023). What have we learned about cues to deception? A survey of expert opinions. Psychology, Crime & Law, 31(5), 511-530.
Meissner, C. A., & Kassin, S. M. (2002). 'He's guilty!': investigator bias in judgments of truth and deception. Law and Human Behavior, 26(5), 469-480. Quoted from the abstract at PubMed.
National Research Council (2003). The Polygraph and Lie Detection. Washington, DC: National Academies Press. Executive summary read for the screening figures quoted here.
Hatz, J. L., & Bourgeois, M. J. (2010). Anger as a cue to truthfulness. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 46(4), 680-683. Located during this check and not read.
